title_en: From the Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews
author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen is commenting on the Epistle to the Hebrews and addressing the question of its authorship and style, since it was traditionally attributed to Paul but differs from his usual manner of writing.
argument: Origen observes that the Greek style of the Epistle to the Hebrews is more polished than Paul's admitted plainness of speech, though its thoughts are worthy of an apostle. He therefore suggests that the ideas are Paul's, but the wording and composition belong to someone who recorded the apostle's teaching and as it were made notes on what was said by the teacher. He allows that any church which receives the epistle as Paul's may be commended, since the ancients handed it down as Paul's, but he says that only God knows who actually wrote it. He reports that some tradition says Clement of Rome wrote it, while others say Luke, the author of the Gospel and Acts.

outline.move: Origen notes that the style of Hebrews is more Greek than Paul's admitted plainness of speech, while its thoughts are not inferior to the acknowledged apostolic writings.
He proposes that the thoughts are Paul's, but the wording and composition belong to someone who recorded the apostle's teaching and as it were made notes on what was said by the teacher.
He says a church that holds Hebrews as Paul's may be approved, since the ancients handed it down as Paul's, but only God knows who wrote it.
He reports the tradition that either Clement of Rome or Luke wrote the epistle.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle who confessed himself to be untrained in speech, and to whom the Epistle to the Hebrews was traditionally attributed.

cast.name: Clement of Rome
cast.who: An early bishop of Rome, named by some as the possible writer of Hebrews.

cast.name: Luke
source_forms: Λουκᾶς ὁ γράψας τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, καὶ τὰς Πράξεις
cast.who: The evangelist and author of Acts, named by others as the possible writer of Hebrews.

voices.speaker: Origen
voices.how_marked: The main voice of the homily, speaking in the first person (Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀποφαινόμενος εἴποιμ' ἄν, 'I speaking my opinion would say').

key_terms.sense: The distinctive character or stamp of the wording or style.
Paul's self-description as untrained or plain in speech.
The wording or expression, as distinct from the thoughts.
The composition or arrangement of the language.
The thoughts or ideas contained in the epistle.
Someone who recorded or wrote down from memory the apostle's teaching.
Someone who wrote notes or comments on what the teacher said.
A local church community that possesses and uses this epistle.
The early Christian authorities who handed down the epistle as Paul's.
The tradition or account that has reached Origen about the epistle's authorship.

scripture: The author refers to the Epistle to the Hebrews and to the Gospel and Acts of Luke. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names: Hebrews, Luke, Acts. No LXX/Vulgate-specific numbering issues arise in this fragment.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the fragment.
The addressee of the homily is not identified in the fragment.
The precise identity of the person Origen thinks recorded Paul's teaching is not given; he only reports traditions naming Clement or Luke.

_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen is commenting on the Epistle to the Hebrews, noting that its Greek style is more polished than Paul's admitted plainness of speech, and addressing questions of its authorship

_unresolved_facts.claim: He therefore suggests that the ideas are Paul's, but the wording and composition belong to someone who recorded the apostle's teaching and as it were made notes on what was said by the teacher
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen states this as his own opinion (Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀποφαινόμενος εἴποιμ' ἄν, 'I speaking my opinion would say'), not as a tentative suggestion

_unresolved_facts.fix: He reports that the tradition that has reached us (ἡ εἰς ἡμᾶς φθάσασα ἱστορία) says that according to some Clement wrote it, according to others Luke

_unresolved_facts.claim: Origen notes that the style of Hebrews is more Greek than Paul's admitted plainness of speech
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen notes that the style of Hebrews is more Greek (ἑλληνικωτέρα), not merely 'more Greek than Paul's admitted plainness of speech'—the comparative is absolute, not explicitly comparative to Paul
